implementation_notes: Dispatch ships the permit primitive: DispatchSemaphore(value: n) per dependency, wait(timeout:) for the bounded wait - .now() is the fail-fast path and returns .timedOut - and signal() in a defer so every exit path releases the slot; it works from synchronous and asynchronous code alike. In Swift concurrency, however, waiting blocks a cooperative thread, so keep guarded sections short, never wait on the main actor, and prefer an async limiter or the OperationQueue variant for longer work.

variants.name: DispatchSemaphore permit
variants.implementation_notes: Dispatch ships the permit primitive: DispatchSemaphore(value: n) per dependency, wait(timeout:) for the bounded wait - .now() is the fail-fast path and returns .timedOut - and signal() in a defer so every exit path releases the slot; it works from synchronous and asynchronous code alike. variants.idiom_name: DispatchSemaphore(value:) with wait(timeout:) and defer signal
pitfalls: Waiting on a DispatchSemaphore from the main thread or the main actor deadlocks the UI; always use a timeout and never block the main thread.
signal() without a matching successful wait inflates the semaphore beyond its initial value and silently removes the bound.
In Swift concurrency, blocking a cooperative thread with wait() can starve the global pool; keep guarded regions short or move them off the pool.
Semaphores are not cancellation-aware: a cancelled Task still holds its slot until the defer runs, so pair them with timeouts.

variants.name: OperationQueue with maxConcurrentOperationCount
variants.implementation_notes: Foundation's OperationQueue is a bounded worker set with its own waiting queue: set maxConcurrentOperationCount = n and add operations for one dependency, so at most n run at a time and the rest wait; it is the direct analogue of a thread-pool bulkhead, supports priorities and dependencies and works with Objective-C APIs. Prefer it over DispatchSemaphore when a synchronous call should run off the caller entirely, and bound or cancel queued operations yourself because the queue itself is unbounded.
pitfalls: The operation queue is unbounded: a slow dependency accumulates operations and their captured state unless operationCount is checked and requests are rejected.
maxConcurrentOperationCount still runs operations on the shared pool, so it is a soft thread bound; target a dedicated dispatch queue for harder isolation.
Operations retain their closure state until executed, so cancelling the queue does not release already-queued work.
Bridging to async/await requires a continuation; a Task started inside an operation does not count toward the queue's concurrency limit.
